topic.subject: science
topic.title: Light: reflection and refraction
topic.scope: spherical mirrors, mirror formula, refraction, refractive index, lenses, lens formula, power of a lens

misconceptions.statement: The image formed by a mirror is located on the surface of the mirror.
misconceptions.why: Students see the reflection 'on' the glass and do not perceive the depth of the virtual or real image.
misconceptions.fix: The image is located at the point where reflected rays actually meet or appear to meet, which is usually behind or in front of the mirror.

probe.question: If you move closer to a plane mirror, where does your image move?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays on the glass surface.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you see is where it is
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on children's ideas

misconceptions.statement: Virtual images cannot be seen because they are not real.
misconceptions.why: The word 'virtual' in everyday language implies something that doesn't exist or is fake.
misconceptions.fix: Virtual images can be seen by the eye because the eye's lens converges the diverging rays onto the retina.

probe.question: Can you see your own reflection in a mirror? Is it real or virtual?
probe.wrong_answer: I can see it, so it must be a real image.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The object distance 'u' is always positive because the object is a real physical thing.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse physical existence with the mathematical sign convention.
misconceptions.fix: According to the Cartesian sign convention, the object is placed to the left of the mirror, making 'u' always negative.

probe.question: An object is 10cm from a mirror. What value of 'u' do you use in the formula?

misconceptions.root_belief: positive numbers represent real physical presence

misconceptions.statement: A negative magnification means the image is smaller than the object.
misconceptions.why: In mathematics, negative numbers are smaller than positive numbers.
misconceptions.fix: In optics, the negative sign indicates the image is inverted; the numerical value indicates the size.

probe.question: If magnification is -2, is the image enlarged or diminished?

misconceptions.statement: Light bends inside the second medium, not at the boundary.
misconceptions.why: Students often draw curved paths or delayed bending in ray diagrams.
misconceptions.fix: Refraction is the change in direction that occurs exactly at the interface of two media with different optical densities.

probe.question: Where does light change its path when entering water from air?
probe.wrong_answer: After it has traveled a few centimeters into the water.

misconceptions.root_belief: processes happen over space not instantly

misconceptions.statement: A higher refractive index means light travels faster in that medium.
misconceptions.fix: Refractive index is inversely proportional to the speed of light; higher index means slower speed.

probe.question: Medium A has n=1.5 and Medium B has n=1.3. In which medium is light faster?

misconceptions.statement: If you cover the top half of a lens, you will only see the bottom half of the image.
misconceptions.why: Students believe each part of the lens is responsible for a specific part of the object.
misconceptions.fix: Every part of the lens forms the whole image; covering half only reduces the brightness of the full image.

probe.question: What happens to the image of a tree if you block the upper half of the lens with black paper?
probe.wrong_answer: The top of the tree disappears from the image.

misconceptions.root_belief: parts of cause create parts of effect

misconceptions.statement: Light rays stop at the point where the image is formed.
misconceptions.why: Ray diagrams usually end at the image point, leading to the belief that light is 'consumed'.
misconceptions.fix: Light rays continue to travel past the image point unless blocked by a screen.

probe.question: If you place your eye exactly at the image position of a real image, what do you see?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, because the light has stopped there.

misconceptions.root_belief: the end of a diagram is the end of the process

misconceptions.statement: A lens with a higher power has a longer focal length.
misconceptions.fix: Power is the reciprocal of focal length (P=1/f); a powerful lens bends light more and has a short focal length.

probe.question: Which lens is more powerful: one with f=10cm or f=20cm?

misconceptions.root_belief: more of A means more of B

misconceptions.statement: The lens formula is exactly the same as the mirror formula.
misconceptions.why: The formulas look very similar and students fail to distinguish the sign between terms.
misconceptions.fix: The mirror formula uses addition (1/v + 1/u) while the lens formula uses subtraction (1/v - 1/u).

probe.question: Write the relationship between u, v, and f for a thin convex lens.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one context works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Focal length is the distance from the object to the mirror's focus.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the 'focus' as a point relative to the object rather than the mirror.
misconceptions.fix: Focal length is the fixed distance between the Pole of the mirror and its Principal Focus.

probe.question: If you move the object further away, what happens to the focal length of the mirror?

misconceptions.root_belief: properties of objects depend on their surroundings

misconceptions.statement: Light only refracts when it enters a liquid like water.
misconceptions.why: Common classroom examples often use water or glass blocks, and air is seen as 'nothing'.
misconceptions.fix: Refraction occurs whenever light passes between any two media of different optical densities, including air to glass or air to oil.

probe.question: Does light bend when it passes from air into a solid diamond?
probe.wrong_answer: No, refraction only happens in liquids.

misconceptions.root_belief: only specific materials have specific properties

misconceptions.statement: Concave lenses can form real images if the object is placed very far away.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the behavior of concave mirrors to concave lenses.
misconceptions.fix: A concave lens always produces a virtual, erect, and diminished image regardless of the object's position.

probe.question: Where should you place an object to get a real image from a concave lens?

misconceptions.statement: Convex mirrors are used in solar furnaces to concentrate sunlight.
misconceptions.why: Confusion between the terms 'convex' and 'concave' and their converging/diverging properties.
misconceptions.fix: Concave mirrors are converging and used in solar furnaces; convex mirrors are diverging.

probe.question: Which mirror would you use to start a fire using sunlight?
probe.wrong_answer: A convex mirror because it is curved outwards.

misconceptions.root_belief: words that sound similar are interchangeable

misconceptions.statement: Light slows down in glass because it has to weave through the atoms.
misconceptions.why: Students apply macroscopic mechanical intuition (like walking through a crowd) to light.
misconceptions.fix: Light slows down due to the interaction of the electromagnetic wave with the electrons of the medium, not by physical 'weaving'.

probe.question: Why is the speed of light less in glass than in vacuum?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the atoms in glass block the straight path of light.

misconceptions.root_belief: macroscopic mechanics apply to subatomic particles

problems: misconception dropped: 'A higher refractive index means light travels fast'
